To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

CEOs of medium-sized private firms are less strategic than other people, but more cooperative, and that CEOs’ strategic choices are more influenced by their own preferences than their beliefs about others.
CEOs are less selfish, more cooperative, less competitive, and more trusting.
CEOs are more cooperative than others in strategic games and that they are less able to predict the behavior of others.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether CEOs are different from others.
the question of how the behavior of CEOs differs from that of others in strategic decision making.
the question whether CEOs are better at making strategic decisions than others and whether they are better at anticipating the strategic decisions of others.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CEOs are more cooperative than others, but they are also more selfish, more risk averse and less strategic than others.
CEOs are more cooperative and less hawkish than other people, and that their beliefs are more optimistic.
CEOs are more cooperative, less hawkish and earn more in these strategic games.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the CEOs in our study behave as though they are more experienced in strategic decision making than the people in our control group.
CEOs are more cooperative and optimistic than others.
CEOs are more trusting than other people and that they are willing to pay a price for this trust, which is a very valuable asset in business life.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the strategic behavior of CEOs differs substantially from that of others.
the CEOs’ decisions and beliefs differ from the control group’s decisions and beliefs in ways that suggest that they are better at strategic decision making.
CEOs are more cooperative and less competitive than comparable people in the general population.
